note: Not a pudding. Never a pudding. Blackberry jam instead of raspberry, which Bakewell need never know about.
Nettle tea. Tastes green, does you good, and nobody gets stung once it's brewed.
Nettle and elderflower in a proper flask. Mum's own blend. Don't tell the corner shop.
Wild garlic, bruised and bottled. One sniff and anyone's wide awake. Possibly for days.
Flaky pastry round a fruity middle. The money's for the butter.
Nettle twine woven tight and padded with wool. Just like the shop ones, only itchier.
A wicker snare re-bent round hazel. Hedgerow creatures feel right at home in it.
Rowan berries tied with red wool. Gran swore by it. Keeps the Night-folk off.
Scones, cream and hedgerow jam. Jam first. We are in Bath, not Devon, and nobody's fighting about it today.
A proper crimp down the side. The money's for the beef. The mushrooms are for flavour, and for showing off.
A little pot with a seaweed lure. Brook and Tide creatures always have a nose.
A holed stone on a cord, wrapped in weed and glass. Look through it and you see the spirits. They see you too.
A slate-backed lamp with a beeswax wick. Peat to light it. Stone creatures dig harder by it.
Speckled bread: fruit soaked overnight in tea. Butter optional, opinions compulsory.
Oats, cream, honey and a splash of something. The something stays in the cupboard for you.
Sugar, butter, honey, and the dentist's phone number.
A wool thistle on a thorn pin. Wha daur meddle wi' me? Nobody, once they've been stabbed by it.
Tea brack with a ring baked in. Whoever finds it is getting married. Or going to the dentist.
Woven on the first of February, hung over the door. Nothing nasty sticks to whoever carries one.
Three green leaves on a pin. A little luck, a little healing, every single turn.
Sticky oat and ginger cake. Best a week old, which nobody has ever managed.
Sugar, peppermint, and a bit of wild honeycomb. Got people up Everest, so it'll get your lot off the floor.
Stew, but don't call it stew. Mushrooms if the lamb's dear. Red cabbage on the side, or else.
Quartered soda bread on a griddle, with a bit of green through it. Fry it in the morning.
Elderflower cordial, let down with spring water. Clears the head and every ailment going.
An acorn from the Major Oak's own line, polished with truffle oil. Steady as an old tree.
Forged hot on a peat fire with an ammonite set in the crown. Points up, so the luck doesn't run out.
Sea glass wrapped in weed and left on the tideline one night. In the morning, it's a pearl. Don't ask who swapped it.
Oatmeal batter left to bubble, then poured on a hot plate and flipped once. Roll round cheese. Eat warm. Repeat.
Dundee jute twine, twisted tight the way the mill spinners did it. One snare from two hanks and a few pence for the twisting, and nobody needs to find a nettle.
Layer it, lid it, forget it for three hours. The potatoes on top go crisp and the bottom goes gravy. Mushrooms if the lamb's dear.
Hot fat, cold batter, and a closed oven door. It rises like a pantomime villain.
Lamb, leeks and whatever root veg the garden gave up. Better on day two. Better still on day three.
Pearl barley, carrot, turnip and a bit of lamb on the bone. Warms you from the toes up.
Smoked haddock, potato, onion and milk. Named for Cullen, up the coast. A skink was once a shin of beef; nobody can say why it became fish.
Pastry, a layer of jam, then an almond-flavoured egg custard poured over. A pudding, not a tart, and don't let anyone tell you otherwise.
Haggis with mashed neeps (that's swede) and tatties (that's potato). Burns Night supper, and a fine one on any other night too.
Bacon, sausage, egg, soda farl and potato bread, all fried in one pan. Breakfast, and also dinner.
Grated raw potato and mash, fried flat. The old rhyme says if you can't make boxty, you'll never get a man. Nobody says that at the table now.
Mash with kale or cabbage and a lake of butter in the middle. Traditionally a ring went in at Hallowe'en, for luck in love.
Laver seaweed boiled for hours into a dark paste, then fried with oatmeal. Welsh caviar, they say. Good on toast with bacon.
Haddock tied in pairs and hot-smoked over hardwood in a half-barrel. Eat it warm, off the bone, with butter. It is the real thing only if it's from Arbroath.
Mash with chopped spring onions and a well of butter in the middle. Eat it from the outside in, dipping.
Mutton or lamb, potatoes and onions, and water. Carrots are a modern heresy, apparently.
Sausages, rashers, onions and potatoes, gently coddled in a pot. A Dublin Saturday-night dish for after the pub.
A spiced fruit pudding boiled in a cloth (a clootie) and dried off in the oven for a skin. A slice, fried, is a good breakfast the next day.
A long, peppery, coarse sausage coiled like a rope, and sold by the length, not the link. Don't cut it up before cooking.
Caerphilly cheese, leek and breadcrumbs, rolled in a sausage shape and fried. No meat at all, and nobody misses it.
Little currant cakes on a bakestone, sugar on top. The smell drifts. Neighbours turn up, and so does everything else.
Potatoes and onions slowly stewed in fat, with last night's leftovers. Served with oatcakes. It tastes better the worse it looks.
Flour, buttermilk and bread soda, with a cross cut on top to let the fairies out. Done in forty minutes with no yeast.
Little Manx queen scallops, the queenies, pan-fried in butter with a bit of garlic. Quick, sweet and gone in a minute.
A big flat round Geordie loaf, dense and chewy, split and stuffed with ham and pease pudding.
